opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think System 1 and System 2 is a useful metaphor, but I'd be careful about taking it too literally. It comes from Kahneman's work on human cognition: System 1 is fast, intuitive, reactive, and System 2 is slow, deliberate, reasoning-heavy. In robotics, a lot of people map this onto a hierarchy. You have a large vision-language model at the top doing high-level reasoning, like "what should I do next, what's the plan," running at maybe a few hertz. Then you have a low-level visuomotor policy at the bottom producing actions at tens or hundreds of hertz, handling contact, closing the loop on perception.

I think there's real engineering truth there. Physical interaction has very different timescales. If you're wiping a table or inserting a peg, you need tight feedback control. You can't wait for a big model to think for two seconds before every motor command. But deciding to clean the kitchen, or figuring out that you need to open the drawer before grabbing the spoon, doesn't need to happen at 100 hertz. So separating frequency and abstraction level makes a lot of sense computationally.

Where I push back a little is the idea that these are two cleanly separable modules, with all the "intelligence" in System 2 and System 1 as a dumb executor. In humans, a lot of what looks like fast intuition is actually very sophisticated. It's compiled experience. A skilled chef isn't reasoning step by step about knife angles. That knowledge has been distilled into motor skill. And the boundary moves: when you first learn to drive, everything is System 2, and after a year most of it is System 1. So the more interesting question to me isn't "how do we bolt a reasoning model onto a control policy," but how knowledge flows between the two. How does slow deliberation get distilled into fast skill over time? And when does the fast system recognize it's out of its depth and escalate to slower reasoning?

There's also the interface problem, which I think is underappreciated. If the high-level system talks to the low-level system in language, like "pick up the red cup," you lose a lot. Language is a pretty lossy bottleneck for physical intent: how to grasp, how much force, what to avoid. So people are exploring richer intermediate representations, like keypoints, trajectories, object-centric goals, or learned latent embeddings. I think the choice of that interface is maybe the most important design decision in these hierarchical systems.

And the last thing is data. System 2-style reasoning benefits enormously from internet-scale pretraining. We have tons of text and video about what people do and why. System 1 for robots needs embodied data: actions, forces, contact. That's much scarcer. So part of why the split exists right now is pragmatic. We use the part that can leverage web data for reasoning, and we spend our precious robot data on the low-level skills. Long term, I'd expect the line to blur, toward more unified models that can think fast or slow depending on the situation, rather than two fixed boxes.

So, a useful framework and a good engineering starting point, but I see it as a spectrum and a learning process, not a fixed architecture.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against treating the systems as cleanly separable, but does not suggest that LLM availability is causing researchers to take the framework too literally.

r002.rationale: The response says embodied data is scarce and anticipates more unified models, but does not say that enough data could support rebuilding physical-action models from scratch instead of grounding an existing LLM.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a useful metaphor, but I'd be careful about treating it as an architectural blueprint. When people in robotics talk about System 1 and System 2, they usually mean something like: there's a fast, reactive, almost reflexive layer that handles low-level control, and then there's a slower, deliberative layer that does planning, reasoning, maybe language understanding. And that maps pretty naturally onto how we've historically built robot systems, right? You have a controller running at a hundred hertz or a thousand hertz, and then some high-level planner sitting on top that decides what to do next.

What I like about the framework is that it forces you to think about time scales and about what kind of computation should happen where. Not every decision needs to be made with a giant model doing chain-of-thought. If you're catching a falling object or recovering from a slip, you don't have time to deliberate. So the question of "what should be amortized into fast, learned reflexes, and what should remain slow and deliberate" is a really productive question.

Where I get a little uncomfortable is when people take the dichotomy too literally, like there must be two separate modules and a clean handoff between them. In practice, I think the boundary is blurry and it moves. Things that start out as System 2, things you have to reason through carefully, get compiled down into System 1 over time with experience. That's what skill acquisition is. A new driver is thinking about every lane change; an experienced driver isn't. So I'd rather think of it as a continuum, where the interesting research question is how you move things along that spectrum, how you distill slow deliberation into fast policies, and when you should escalate back up because the fast policy is out of distribution.

The other thing I'd add is that in the physical world, the slow system can't just sit there and think. The world keeps moving. So System 2 for an embodied agent has to be interruptible, it has to reason about its own latency, and it has to be okay with the fast layer doing something sensible in the meantime. That's quite different from a language model answering a question where it can take as long as it wants. So the framework is a good starting point, but the embodied setting adds constraints that I think push you toward something more integrated than the clean two-system picture suggests.

r001.rationale: The response says people can take the System 1/System 2 distinction too literally, but does not connect that tendency to the availability of LLMs.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether sufficient data could enable rebuilding physical-action models from scratch instead of grounding an existing LLM.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful framework, especially for robotics, because you need to operate at very different timescales. If you’re picking up a cup and it starts slipping, you need to react immediately. You can’t stop and reason through every possible action. That’s the System 1 side: a policy that maps what you perceive into an action very quickly.

But if you’re trying to make dinner, you also need to think about what to do first, what tools you need, and what to do when something isn’t available. That’s closer to System 2: reasoning over a longer horizon and breaking a goal into things you can execute.

The interesting question is how those two interact. The planner might say, ‘Pick up the cup,’ but the controller might discover that it can’t reach it. That information needs to flow back so the plan can change. And you need to decide when to keep acting and when to pause and think.

So I find the distinction helpful as a design intuition. But naming one component System 1 and another System 2 doesn’t solve the problem. The hard part is connecting reasoning to what the robot can actually perceive and do.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the distinction a useful design intuition and says naming components does not solve the problem; it does not suggest that LLM availability is leading researchers to take the framework too literally.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses connecting reasoning to a robot’s perceptions and actions, but does not mention sufficient data, rebuilding models from scratch, or grounding an existing LLM in action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful framework, especially for robotics, as long as we don’t take the analogy too literally. There are things a robot needs to do quickly—respond to contact, adjust its grasp, keep moving smoothly—and there are things that benefit from more deliberation, like figuring out how to approach an unfamiliar task or recovering when a plan fails.

You can think of those as System 1 and System 2. But the interesting question is how they work together. You don’t want a robot to reason through every motor command, and you also don’t want it to keep executing a learned behavior when the situation has changed. It needs some way to recognize, “This is outside what I can handle reliably; I should slow down and reconsider.”

And in the physical world, that deliberation has to stay grounded in feedback. You can make a very plausible plan, but then you reach for an object and it slips. So it’s not simply planning first and acting afterward. It’s a continuous interaction between deciding what to do, doing it, and observing what actually happened.

r001.rationale: The candidate cautions against taking the analogy too literally, but does not say LLM availability is causing researchers to do so.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss whether sufficient data could enable rebuilding physical-action models from scratch instead of grounding an existing LLM.
